summary: A first-person narrator describes leaving formal school behind and how they handled schooling, including altering records to enter the intended grade rather than repeat one, and finding comfort studying at University of Minnesota libraries from age fourteen. The narrator contrasts school's structure with college life, mentions a program letting high schoolers take college classes with free textbooks that they plan to try at sixteen, and notes being busy with a business and 'the Group.' The excerpt closes with a dialogue between the narrator and Monica about Wilson, whose family's home was raided on the news.
one_line: A teenage narrator recounts leaving conventional school for University of Minnesota libraries and plans for a college-credit program, while Monica and the narrator discuss Wilson's raided home on the news.
key_facts: The narrator altered records after changing schools so they could enter the grade they were supposed to be going into instead of repeating the one they never finished.
The narrator says that taking a GED test would have been simpler, but that option was not available to them.
The narrator describes school as 'a prison system combined with a mass babysitting operation.'
The narrator started hanging out at the libraries at the University of Minnesota after hitting fourteen, citing guest wifi and no little kids screaming as in the public library.
The narrator reports that articles found on Google Scholar cost thirty-five bucks but are free using a library computer.
The narrator felt comfortable in the university libraries, 'like just another college student.'
A student told the narrator about a program where high school kids could take college classes and even get free textbooks.
The narrator planned to apply for that program next year when they would be sixteen and eligible.
The narrator says they had their own business to run, had 'the Group,' and did not miss going to a regular school at all.
Monica says 'Wilson's father must be going crazy' while staring at a picture of kids being led out of a house.
In the news picture, Wilson walks in front, looking like he just woke up and wondering why people with guns are in his front yard.
Monica's line, 'how embarrassing, my kid's on the news? What will people think?', is a mocking imitation of Wilson's father's presumed reaction.
